\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\title{Minimum Wages and Employment in Border Counties: New Evidence}
\author{L.~Brandt and S.~Okoye}
\date{March 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
We revisit the employment effects of minimum-wage increases using
county-level panel data from paired border counties between 2011 and 2024.
Across four specifications we find small negative employment responses
concentrated in accommodation and food services.
The estimates are stable to sector fixed effects, region-specific trends,
and an instrument based on lagged statutory exposure.
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}
The employment effect of the minimum wage remains one of the oldest
disputes in labor economics.
Canonical case studies of paired counties reported near-zero effects,
while panel-data estimates have often been negative and sizable.
This paper revisits the dispute with thirteen years of county-level data
and a design that compares each treated county with its immediate neighbor.
We focus on the accommodation and food-services sector, where minimum-wage
workers are concentrated, while also reporting economy-wide responses.
Our contribution is twofold.
First, we extend the paired-county design through the 2024 recovery,
a period with large and frequent statutory increases.
Second, we provide an instrumental-variables estimate that uses lagged
statutory exposure in neighboring states as a source of plausibly
exogenous variation.
The results point to employment responses that are negative but small,
and considerably smaller than the older panel-data literature suggested.
\section{Data}
We assemble a quarterly county panel from 2011 to 2024.
Employment and earnings come from administrative records aggregated to
the county-sector level.
Minimum-wage schedules are coded from state statutes and local ordinances,
including scheduled increases that were later postponed.
Border pairs are defined as adjacent counties that straddle a state line
and share a metropolitan labor market.
After excluding pairs affected by a statewide reclassification in 2016,
the estimation sample covers 312 county pairs.
Descriptive statistics confirm that treated and control counties moved
in parallel before the first increase in our window.
The average statutory minimum rose by 42 percent over the sample period,
with substantial variation across pairs in both timing and level.
\section{Empirical Strategy}
The baseline specification regresses log sectoral employment on the log
of the statutory minimum wage, with county-pair and quarter fixed effects.
We then add sector fixed effects interacted with time, region-specific
linear trends, and finally an instrument that exploits lagged exposure.
Standard errors are clustered at the state level throughout.
All regressions are weighted by county-sector employment in 2011.
\section{Results}
Table \ref{tab:wage} collects the four headline specifications.
The baseline estimate implies that a ten percent increase in the minimum
wage lowers sectoral employment by about 0.4 percent.
The estimate shrinks modestly as fixed effects and trends are added,
and the instrumental-variables estimate is the smallest of the four.
None of the specifications produces an economy-wide response that is
statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional levels.
\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|c|c|c|}
\hline
Specification & Coefficient & Std.\ error & $p$-value \\
\hline
Baseline OLS & -0.042 & 0.011 & 0.002 \\
With sector fixed effects & -0.038 & 0.010 & 0.004 \\
With region trends & -0.031 & 0.009 & 0.006 \\
IV with lagged exposure & -0.027 & 0.012 & 0.031 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\caption{Estimated effect of the minimum-wage reform on log employment.}
\label{tab:wage}
\end{table}
Event-study estimates show no pre-trend in the five years before the
first increase, which supports the identifying assumption.
Effects are concentrated in limited-service restaurants and are close
to zero in retail and in manufacturing.
Teen employment responds more strongly than prime-age employment,
although the teen estimates are imprecise.
\section{Discussion}
The estimates reconcile part of the gap between case-study and
panel-data findings: responses are negative but small, and they are
concentrated where theory predicts.
Two caveats deserve emphasis.
First, county-level aggregation may mask displacement across neighboring
sectors within a county.
Second, our window ends in 2024, and the effects of the largest scheduled
increases may not yet be fully realized.
\section{Conclusion}
Using thirteen years of paired-county data, we estimate minimum-wage
employment elasticities that are negative, small, and stable across
specifications.
The magnitudes imply that the increases observed in our window raised
earnings for low-wage workers at modest employment cost.
Whether the same holds for the substantially larger increases now
scheduled in several states is a question for future work.
\end{document}
